summaries.example: Imagine 21 students choosing a class helper: 8 rank A first, 7 rank B first, and 6 rank C first. A looks strongest by first-place votes. But many students rank A last. In one-on-one contests, C beats A, B, and D, while B beats D and has strong overall support. A method that counts first choices might choose A; a method that compares every pair might choose C; a method that adds points for all positions might choose B.
summaries.summary: Voting methods are different procedures for turning many people’s opinions into a group decision. A simple rule counts only first-place votes. Other rules use full rankings, grades, approvals, or several rounds. The same set of opinions can produce different winners under different procedures. The entry explains why this happens and examines ways to compare methods. It also describes voting paradoxes: situations where a rule behaves in a surprising way, such as making a candidate lose after receiving more support. A central lesson is that no single method is best in every situation. Choosing a method involves deciding what matters most, such as ease of use, fairness, resistance to tricks, or the ability to show strong and weak preferences.
key_ideas: Groups often disagree, so there may be no single obvious winner.
Different voting methods can choose different winners from exactly the same votes.
Plurality chooses the candidate with the most first-place votes, but it can choose someone who loses every one-on-one contest.
Borda Count gives points for all ranking positions, while methods such as approval voting let voters support more than one candidate.
Voting theory studies useful rules, surprising problems called paradoxes, and the trade-offs among fairness, simplicity, and how much voters can express.
summaries.why_it_matters: Voting rules affect decisions in classrooms, clubs, committees, and larger elections. Learning about them helps us see that “the group’s choice” is not produced by votes alone; it also depends on the counting rule. Careful comparison can reveal what a method makes easy to express and what problems it may create.

important_terms.definition: A rule for combining people’s votes to choose one winner, several winners, or an order of choices.
A voter’s way of showing an opinion, such as choosing one candidate, ranking candidates, or giving grades.
A contest between two choices. The choice preferred by more voters wins that contest.
A candidate who defeats every other candidate in one-on-one elections.
A method that gives points for places in a ranking. For example, first place can receive more points than second place.

questions_to_think_about: Should the candidate with the most first-place votes always win?
Is beating every other candidate one-on-one enough to make someone the best group choice?
Would you rather rank every choice or give each choice a grade?
Why might two reasonable voting rules choose different winners?

summaries.example: Use the 21-voter profile with rankings A>B>C>D for 3 voters, A>C>B>D for 5, B>D>C>A for 7, and C>B>D>A for 6. A has the most first-place votes, but A is ranked last by 13 voters and loses head-to-head contests against each other candidate. C defeats A 13–8, B 11–10, and D 14–7, so C is the Condorcet winner. B, however, has the highest Borda score because it performs strongly across all positions. Thus Condorcet reasoning favors C, while a positional scoring rule favors B.
summaries.summary: The entry presents voting as a problem of aggregating individual opinions into a collective decision. A voting method takes a profile of ballots and returns a winner, a set of tied winners, or sometimes an ordering. Methods differ in what ballots communicate. Plurality records only a top choice; ranking methods use positions; approval and grading methods allow voters to mark several candidates or express evaluations. These choices matter because different methods can yield different outcomes from the same profile. Condorcet’s approach looks for a candidate who beats every rival in pairwise majority contests. Borda Count instead awards position-based points and rewards broad support. Neither perspective settles every case: a Condorcet winner may not exist, and Borda need not select one when it does exist. The entry develops criteria for comparison, including practical simplicity, information conveyed, anonymity, neutrality, unanimity, monotonicity, and reinforcement. It then examines paradoxes, strategic voting, impossibility and characterization theorems, truth-tracking interpretations, and computational social choice. The broad conclusion is not that all methods are equally good, but that each embodies choices and faces trade-offs; no method is best in all situations.
key_ideas: Voting methods differ in the information they request: a single choice, a ranking, approvals, grades, or delegated influence.
Plurality is simple but can elect a Condorcet loser. Borda Count uses more ranking information but need not elect a Condorcet winner.
A Condorcet winner need not exist because majority comparisons can cycle, even when every individual ranking is consistent.
Voting methods can violate desirable properties such as monotonicity, participation, or reinforcement; these failures are studied through voting paradoxes.

Axiomatic results characterize methods using principles such as anonymity, neutrality, unanimity, reinforcement, and continuity. May’s theorem singles out majority rule for two alternatives, while Arrow’s theorem shows that demanding several strong conditions for three or more alternatives creates an impossibility.
The entry also considers epistemic questions—whether voting can track a correct answer—and computational questions about calculating winners or manipulating elections.
summaries.why_it_matters: Elections do not simply reveal a pre-existing group preference. A rule helps construct the collective result from incomplete and sometimes conflicting information. Understanding voting methods therefore matters for democratic design and for smaller decisions in committees or organizations. It also teaches a wider philosophical lesson: reasonable principles can conflict, and a procedure’s mathematical behavior may differ from its intuitive promise.

important_terms.definition: The formal study of procedures that aggregate individual ballots into a collective decision.
A profile in which each voter submits a ballot; a ballot may be a choice, ranking, subset, or set of grades.
A candidate who defeats every other candidate by majority in pairwise comparisons.
A candidate who loses every pairwise comparison with the other candidates.
A rule assigning weights to ranking positions and adding each candidate’s resulting points.
A method that satisfies the condition that an existing Condorcet winner is elected.
A surprising outcome showing that pairwise majority comparisons can form a cycle, such as A defeating B, B defeating C, and C defeating A.
A voting rule in which a voter may submit a ballot that misstates their preferences to improve the expected outcome.

questions_to_think_about: Should a Condorcet winner always defeat a candidate selected by a scoring rule?
Is a voting method better when it gathers more information, or when it is easier for voters to use accurately?
What should count as a serious failure: electing a Condorcet loser, changing the winner after a candidate gains support, or failing to produce a winner?
Why might a method that works well for two alternatives become problematic with three or more?
Can a procedure be fair by its rules yet fail to identify the objectively best decision?

summaries.example: Suppose a student council has four candidates. Some students vote only for their favorite, while others rank all four. A plurality count might choose the candidate with the most first-place votes. But if students compare candidates in pairs, another candidate might defeat each rival. A ranking-points system could choose a third candidate because that person is often second or third rather than being many students’ first choice. These are not counting mistakes. They show that each rule asks a different question about what “best represents the group” means.
summaries.summary: Voting methods are systems for turning individual judgments into a group choice. The source begins with a basic difficulty: disagreement does not always produce one obvious winner, especially when there are several candidates. A ballot may contain only one selected candidate, a complete ranking, a set of approved candidates, or grades. The method then processes the profile of ballots. Plurality selects whoever has the most first-place votes. Borda Count awards points for every ranking position, so it measures wider support. Condorcet’s approach uses pairwise majority contests and favors a candidate who defeats every rival. These approaches can disagree, and sometimes pairwise majority relations cycle: A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A. The entry surveys runoff and elimination methods, approval and grading systems, quadratic voting, and liquid democracy, then asks how rules should be evaluated. Important standards include anonymity, neutrality, unanimity, monotonicity, and reinforcement. Yet desirable standards can conflict. The entry also discusses strategic voting, impossibility results, attempts to use voting to identify truth, and computational questions about finding or manipulating outcomes. Its main message is that voting design requires judgment about competing goals rather than simple discovery of one perfect formula.
key_ideas: The meaning of a group decision depends partly on the voting procedure used to produce it.
Plurality is easy to understand but uses little information and can select a candidate who loses head-to-head contests.
Condorcet and Borda methods represent different ideas of broad support: pairwise victories versus performance across all ranking positions.
With three or more candidates, majority comparisons can cycle, so no candidate may beat every rival.
Methods can be compared by fairness principles, ease of use, information, resistance to manipulation, and how they handle ties and paradoxes.
The source’s overall lesson is comparative: every method has strengths and weaknesses, so there is no universally best rule.
summaries.why_it_matters: A voting rule can change the result even when everyone’s opinions stay the same. That matters in elections, clubs, committees, and any group that must make a shared choice. Studying the rules helps us discuss disagreements more carefully: instead of asking only who won, we can ask what information was used, what principle guided the count, and what trade-offs the procedure creates.

important_terms.definition: A procedure for combining individual opinions into a decision for the whole group.
The information a voter submits, such as one choice, a ranking, approvals, or grades.
A list of all voters’ ballots, including how many people submitted each kind of ballot.
A candidate who wins a majority in a head-to-head contest against every other candidate.
A rule that gives candidates points according to their positions in voters’ rankings.
The idea that giving a candidate more support should not make that candidate worse off.
A surprising result in which a voting procedure behaves contrary to a seemingly reasonable expectation.
Voting in a way designed to obtain a preferred result rather than simply reporting one’s sincere ranking.

questions_to_think_about: Does broad support mean being many voters’ favorite, being acceptable to most voters, or defeating each rival?
Would a rule be fair if it treated voters equally but ignored much of what they said?
Why can adding support for a candidate sometimes change which candidates enter a later round?
Should voters be expected to vote sincerely if a rule rewards strategic behavior?
How should a group choose between a simple method and a more expressive one?
